title: incremental-prefetch-proxy-backpressure-study-sep-2025
content:
Purpose

Quick exploratory run to understand how small, incremental token prefetching from clients interacts with edge proxies and causes (or mitigates) backpressure during LLM streaming. This grew out of support requests where customers reported improvements in first-token latency with an SDK-level prefetch, but worse 95/99 tail under sustained load. We want to attribute where latency moves and propose mitigations.

Motivation / hypothesis
- Hypothesis A: Client-side incremental prefetch (speculatively sending extra prompt/context or pre-request tokens) reduces time-to-first-token when the model needs KV warmup or initial computation.
- Hypothesis B: The same traffic pattern increases egress bursts through proxies (especially ones with small buffer budgets or per-connection fairness rules), amplifying queuing, causing tail latency regressions for co-located streams.
- Secondary: Behavior differs between HTTP/2 (windowing/coalescing) and gRPC (HTTP/2 + framing) and with different proxy implementations (Envoy vs our inproc proxy).

Testbed / environment
- Serving runtime: local cluster of 4 inference nodes (A100 40GB), model: redwood/open-lm-13b-quant (representative KV-warm start), runtime version: serve-v2.4.1 (instrumented).
- Edge: two proxy types: envoy-1.22 (default config) and internal-proxy v0.11 (lightweight, per-connection buffers).
- Clients: synthetic driver that can toggle incremental prefetch window (0, +2, +5 speculative tokens), chunking (immediate flush vs 64B coalesce vs 4KB coalesce), and transport (HTTP/2 direct vs gRPC over HTTP/2).
- Load generator: Poisson arrival, mean concurrency sweep {5, 20, 50} streams, each stream: prompt sizes sampled from production distribution (mostly 32-256 tokens).
- Observability: per-token traces, proxy buffer occupancy, socket send queues (SO_SNDBUF), runtime KV cache misses, CPU on proxies, and tail-latency p50/p95/p99/end-to-end.

Experiment matrix (abridged)
- Prefetch windows: 0, 2, 5
- Chunking: immediate, coalesce-64B, coalesce-4KB
- Transport: http2-direct, grpc
- Proxy: none (direct), envoy, internal-proxy
- Load: low(5), med(20), high(50) concurrent streams

Key metrics collected
- time_to_first_token (ms)
- token_pacing_variance (ms) // inter-token arrival stdev
- p50/p95/p99 overall latency
- proxy_buffer_ms (time token spends queued in proxy)
- proxy_cpu_pct
- kv_warm_miss_rate
- retransmit/packetization events (from tcpdump traces)

Results (summary)
1) Time-to-first-token: incremental prefetch of +2 tokens reduces median TTF by ~18-25% across transports for cold-KV cases. Gains beyond +2 produced diminishing returns.
2) Under low load (5 streams): prefetch had neutral-to-positive effect on all tail metrics; proxy buffering negligible.
3) Under medium load (20 streams): envoy tolerated +2 prefetch with small p95 change (~+5%), but internal-proxy showed p95 regressions up to +35% for immediate flush clients.
4) Under high load (50 streams): +5 prefetch with immediate-flush caused proxy buffer amplification: proxy_buffer_ms increased 3x, p99 latency for unrelated streams increased ~2x on internal-proxy, ~1.3x on Envoy.
5) Chunking/coalescing matters: small coalesce (64B) combined with prefetch reduced proxy buffer spikes by ~20% vs immediate flush. Large coalesce (4KB) reduced spikes further but increased time-to-first-token by ~40ms (bad for user-facing streaming).
6) Transport differences: grpc vs http2-direct produced similar high-level trends, but grpc framing produced slightly burstier socket writes (due to gRPC runtime batching) which made internal-proxy bursts worse.
7) CPU on proxies scaled with burstiness: internal-proxy CPU rose to 70% under high-load+prefetch, indicating scheduling and buffer management pressure.

Observations / interpretation
- Small speculative prefetch windows (1-2 tokens) are net-positive for perceived responsiveness in low-to-medium load; larger speculative windows create short egress microbursts that interact poorly with proxies that have per-connection budgets or do aggressive fairness.
- The mismatch is not just bytes-in-flight: it's timing. Many streams pushing tiny frames in quick succession cause repeated wakeups and scheduler contention in proxy worker threads, amplifying tail latency for other streams on same worker.
- Coalescing at client side (delay 1-2ms to aggregate small writes) is effective at smoothing bursts while keeping TTF reasonable. However, it requires SDK-level changes and careful defaults.
- Envoy is more robust due to connection window heuristics and write coalescing; lighter internal proxy is vulnerable to per-conn buffer saturation and event loop stalls.
- gRPC runtime behavior (internal batching and flush heuristics) can be tuned; default may be suboptimal for speculative prefetch patterns.

Actionable mitigations tested (mini experiments)
- Client pacing: adding a 0.5–2ms pacing between speculative frames reduced p99 spikes by ~30% with minor TTF regression (~10ms). Recommendation: SDK default to soft pacing when prefetch enabled.
- Adaptive prefetch: enable +2 tokens only when client-side signals show KV cold + low concurrency; otherwise disable. Need signals: kv_warm_miss_hint or server profiling hook.
- Proxy-side per-connection write-smoothing: implement a small token-bucket on egress path to spread bursts; prototype reduced tail by 20% but increased CPU. Tradeoff CPU vs latency.
- Coalesce at transport layer: 64–256B coalesce window (1–3ms) seems a practical default.

Open questions / unresolved
- How do these effects change with QUIC/UDP-based transports? (next run) My expectation: QUIC's packet pacing may help but also interact with spin-wait on worker threads differently.
- Can smart routing steer prefetching streams away from lightweight proxies? We could add a tagging signal but that requires routing policy work in control plane.
- How well do these findings hold for much larger models / longer sequences where token production is slower? Bursts may be absorbed more easily if token cadence is lower.

Notes to self / follow-ups
- Add tests with variable RTT (10ms, 50ms) — client-side pacing benefits may be RTT-sensitive.
- File a small SDK change PR: default prefetch +2 with 1ms write-coalesce, add env var to disable. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/1234 (draft).
- Create a short runbook for Support: when customers report worse tails after enabling speculative prefetch, ask about proxy type and concurrency, recommend turning on SDK pacing/coalesce.

Next experiments (planned)
- Run QUIC-enabled proxy variant and repeat high-load matrix (target: Oct 2025).
- Measure kernel-level wakeups (futex/wakeup_count) on proxy under bursts to quantify scheduler effect.
- Integrate server-side kv_warm hints in headers and evaluate adaptive prefetch trigger.

Appendix: quick traces (qualitative)
- Sample trace (high-load, +5 prefetch, immediate flush, internal-proxy): sequence shows repeated small write syscalls from client clustered in <1ms windows, internal-proxy IO thread spikes, epoll wakeups queued, worker stalls ~2-8ms, unrelated stream tokens delayed — explains p99 blowup.
- Sample trace (same but with 1ms client coalesce): writes reduced by ~40%, proxy CPU stable, p99 improved.

If anyone wants raw data or dashboards, ping me (Arun). I'll push cleaned CSVs to the shared bench bucket and add a Grafana dashboard link once I tidy the panels.
